X. On Whether the Innate Evil of the Ultimate Buddha-Stage is Severed or Not Severed Ten Questions by the Great Virtue Dharma Master Tokuen,
Inner Offering Priest of the Tendai Hokke School at Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in Japan.
In the first [chapter] of the Lotus Sutra, it says that sixty *bhojana-muhūrta* (meals' intervals) are equivalent to fifty-five days;

this implies that the "first" refers to the Lotus Sutra. Furthermore, it states that sixty minor *kalpas* (*kṣudra-kalpa*) are like a single meal's interval, while the fifth [chapter] states that fifty minor *kalpas* are like half a day.
It further says that those who have emerged from the earth praise the various Bodhisattvas with diverse hymns.
While praising the Buddha in this manner according to the Dharma, fifty intermediate kalpas passed;

furthermore, the seventh [chapter] states that when he extended his broad and long tongue, emitted immeasurable light, and manifested supernatural powers, a full hundred thousand years elapsed (and so forth).
Now, a doubt arises: while it is said that the Lotus Sūtra was preached over the course of eight years, this present sūtra states that fifty intermediate kalpas passed.
Regarding the phrase "and for hundreds of thousands of years," what is its intended meaning?

If one were to calculate *kalpas* based on days, nights, months, seasons, and years, it would mean eight days and nights, eight months, eight seasons, and eight years. Now, as for the fifty-six minor *kalpas* and the hundreds of thousands of years, what is their underlying intent?
The *Tiantai Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) states: "Fifty minor... [The text continues: "...minor *kalpas*."
That an eon (*kalpa*) and half a day are identical refers to the inconceivability of time.

Furthermore, it is said that for those who understand, the short is perceived as long—meaning fifty minor eons (*antarakalpa*)—while for those who are deluded, the long is perceived as short—meaning it is like half a day.
It is also said that just as worldly people perceive the short as long when suffering and the long as short when joyful, this expresses the resolve to revere the Dharma.
Therefore, it is merely spoken of in terms of time (and so forth). Now, as for the doubt: on the day of the *Lotus Sūtra*, who would be deluded and who would be enlightened?
For one who is deluded and possesses suffering, what is short can be made long; this is called "fifty small kalpas.
For one who is enlightened and possesses joy, what is long can be made short; this is called "half a day. Where do those who emerge from the earth come from?
The assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa reckons fifty minor kalpas as half a day.

Generally speaking, since it is said that inconceivable time allows for fifty minor kalpas to be equivalent to hundreds of thousands of years and so forth—even within eight years, the ten directions and the three periods of time have not yet transcended a single fleeting thought-moment; how much less could they encompass fifty?
A small kalpa (*antarakalpa*) is like half a day; sixty small kalpas are like the duration of a meal—what is there to marvel at?
We know for certain that hundreds of thousands of years are not long, and a meal’s duration or half a day is not short either, because inconceivable time has no fixed length or brevity.
As for what is called "the day of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*," who can explain it, and who can understand it?

Regarding those who are deluded, it is said that at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were already the fourfold assembly of initiators and others, encompassing all those whose delusions had been resolved;

yet, there are seven types of persons possessing a nature of full-blown afflictions who harbor seven kinds of pride, and three types of persons free from afflictions who possess three kinds of defiled pride.
Those who have not heard the teaching on the seven parables and the three equalities are all termed "deluded"; having heard [this], they...

Only upon awakening and understanding can one be called an "understander. All those seeking the Three Vehicles who have not yet received the three turnings of the wheel of the One Vehicle are deluded;

only after hearing [the teaching] and attaining realization can they be called understanders. Furthermore, after the Three Vehicles were opened and the One Vehicle was revealed, those who had not yet heard the *Niyata-āyuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Lifespan) and were thus ignorant of the principle of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment over a vast duration of time were all considered deluded;
only upon hearing the *Niyata-āyuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta* [do they become understanders].

If those who only later come to be called "understanders" are already so designated, how much more so those who, through both the gates of the original and the manifested, respond like shadows to echoes and inwardly contemplate and strike [the bell of truth]?

It is not necessarily the case that the assembly on Vulture Peak were all deluded, nor is it the case that the people who emerged from the earth were not [deluded].
All of these are those who have attained understanding. The reason for this is that on Vulture Peak, they had already awakened to the inconceivable principle of the One Vehicle;

it is therefore fitting that they be considered those who have attained understanding. As for the multitude who emerged from the earth, since they were all beings being transformed [by the Buddha], one truly knows that not all of them necessarily possessed such understanding.

Furthermore, it is not said that the multitude who emerged from the earth [attained understanding], but rather it is said that the multitude on Vulture Peak did so during the fifty intermediate kalpas.
Half a day was merely encompassed [within a longer duration] and described as fifty minor kalpas;
through the Buddha’s supernormal power, he caused the great assembly to perceive it as being like half a day. This is but one aspect of the fundamental inconceivability.

Those who understand do not merely comprehend this, but can also clearly discern how the long is contained within the short, and how the short extends into the long. As for those who are deluded, they merely marvel at how half a day suddenly passed away.
One does not yet know the length of the kalpas traversed, nor can one fathom how half a day could contain the fundamental source of fifty minor kalpas;
how is it that the short becomes long? It is for this reason that the distinction between understanding and delusion arises.

Regarding the confusion concerning the three types of compassion held by others, the general response is as follows:
The essence of the Dharma is fundamentally neither birth-and-death nor nirvana, neither affliction nor enlightenment;
it cannot be said to be identical, nor can it be said to be different. There is no suffering or accumulation to be severed, and no sentient beings to be delivered. It is simply this.

Through false conceptualization and discrimination, one falsely clings to the existence of signs within the signless; within the absence of the accumulation of suffering, one gives rise to the appearance of the accumulation of suffering.
Following these delusive perceptions, the beginningless continuity of one's own accumulated aggregates of suffering causes the cycle of saṃsāra to ceaselessly turn.
Therefore, through the tireless power of the compassion of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Path is provisionally established within that which is beyond verbal expression.

The teaching of cessation is to forcefully apply the names of suffering and its origin within the state where no marks originally exist, in order to deliver sentient beings who have not yet attained quiescent extinction.
One cuts off afflictions that are like empty space; one does not cease from this rescue until the end.

Throughout the day of such cutting, one sees no sentient being to be delivered and no suffering or origin to be severed. Since the marks of suffering and its origin do not exist, [cessation is established].

The principle of the Path that extinguishes [suffering] is fundamentally quiescent; because it realizes that the illusions of suffering and its origin have no substantial reality, it differs from the Tripitaka Teaching.

Because it employs the three contemplations in perfect reflection, it differs from the Shared Teaching. Because it is neither separate from extremes nor sequential, it differs from the Distinct Teaching.
Thus, its perfectly integrated compassion does not overlap with the three preceding teachings.
Regarding the doubt concerning the similarities and differences between the fourth, the Perfect True Reward (*yuan-shi bao*), and the Separate True Reward (*bie-shi bao*):

However, if one infers by way of meaning, the *Vairocana Sūtra* may be subsumed under the fifth period. The reason for this is that within the [first] four flavors..."

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "inclusive" (*kan*) and "corresponding" (*tai*), the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* discusses the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) exclusively, without distinctions such as inclusivity and so forth;
thus, it is even more sublime when one has other scriptural authorities to rely upon. However, among the four teachings, this [sūtra] should be categorized as the Perfect Teaching.
Why, then, does that sūtra state: "Every lifting and lowering of the feet is entirely a mudrā, and all speech is nothing other than direct expression"?
Furthermore, it is said that from the Buddha down to even a scorpion, all are none other than the Dharma-realm body of Vairocana;
this thus accords in profound harmony with the principle of the Perfect [Teaching], wherein every single form and fragrance is the Middle Way.
It is therefore appropriate that this be subsumed within the Perfect Teaching, which is why Master Xingyan employed the principles of the Perfect Teaching entirely to explain the scriptural text.
Regarding the eighth point, the doubt as to whether or not the body produced by ignorance is abandoned at the time of attaining Buddhahood in this very body:
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that an eight-year-old dragon girl emerged from the sea and, in an instant, transformed into a male, perfected the practices of a bodhisattva,
and immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal enlightenment.

The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "At the time when the Buddha manifested these supernatural transformations, ten thousand women manifested the transformation of their female bodies and attained the samādhi of supernormal powers;
immeasurable devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges manifested their bodies as Buddhas. Master Yixing’s *Commentary on the Vairocana Sūtra* states:
There are briefly three analogies for entering the gateway of mantras: first, the gateway of body-secrecy (*kāyaguhyaka*); second, the gateway of speech-secrecy (*vāgguhyaka*);
and third, the gateway of mind-secrecy (*cittaguhyaka*). By means of these three skillful means, one purifies the three karmas of oneself and becomes empowered by the three secrets of the Tathāgata;
thus, one may fulfill the stages and perfections (*bhūmi-pāramitā*) in this very life, without having to undergo further rebirths.

Because one fully cultivates all remedial practices over the course of many kalpas, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that some bodhisattvas, at the very moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], immediately ascend to the bodhisattva stage and attain non-retrogression;

others, at the very moment they first resolve their minds, immediately attain unsurpassed bodhi and are able to turn the wheel of Dharma. The Mantra Vehicle (Shingon) now relies upon the aforementioned passage.
It is said that through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of mantras, one manifests a golden body; this is not a case of discarding this present body to receive another body.

Furthermore, the Mantra School (*Shingon-shū*) states that this interpretation is incorrect, asserting that one must necessarily discard the body produced by ignorance and receive a further, untainted fruit-body (*anāsrava-phala-kāya*) to achieve perfect enlightenment.
As for the teaching of "attaining Buddhahood in this very body" (*sokushin jōbutsu*), it means that the essence is inherently complete within the mind.

The three bodies of equality of Vairocana constitute what is termed "perfect enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); it does not mean that one attains perfect enlightenment through a body manifested in a dream.
If one were to attain perfect enlightenment without casting off this [present] body, how could a dragon girl ascend the lotus pedestal and so forth?
Now, I wonder which of these two positions established by these two schools is correct; furthermore, regarding the *lakṣaṇa-vāda* school (the Abhidharma/Realist school)...
Regarding the statement that "the body of transformation refines tainted retribution to form an untainted body"—how does this compare with the present meaning?
The general response is:
Buddhism has many gateways, and those who enter it each follow what their own minds delight in; thus, whether it be the "body" (soku-shin) or "separation from the body" (ko-se), they are all one.
The vow to attain Buddhahood is like the various streams of water entering the ocean directly to become of one taste;
attaining Buddhahood in this very body (*sokushin jōbutsu*) is brought about by those of superior faculties who suddenly awaken to the perfect principle and practice with diligence.

If one does not practice diligently, those of inferior faculties who awaken gradually cannot avoid being separated from birth after birth; only after passing through kalpas will they finally reach their intended goal and realize what has been traversed.
In an instant, it is like awakening from a dream of a hundred years; there is only a single thought. As the Sūtra says, regarding the transformation of the Dragon Girl’s body into that of a male:
this merely exchanges the female organ of the Dragon Girl for a male form; it does not involve casting off life to undergo a separate rebirth.
The reason for transforming the Dragon Girl’s physical organ is to cause sentient beings to give rise to a mind of respect and to engender deep faith in the Dharma being taught.
Therefore, by transforming inferior faculties into a superior essence, one attains perfect enlightenment.

If one objects that the Buddha with dragon horns is a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) appearing according to the species of beings and thus not permitted to again take the form of one covered in fur and bearing horns—then let us distinguish the similarities and differences between the meaning of "refining the faculties to achieve the outflow-free state" in the *lakṣaṇa* school and "attaining Buddhahood in this very body" in this Perfect Gate (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). In the former case, it concerns practice and understanding...
This is the simultaneous perfection of both practice and realization.
Regarding the ninth point—whether insentient objects such as grass and trees attain Buddhahood and preach the Dharma—the *Yizhi Guanzhong Yili* states:
"Because the Buddha-vehicle is established within the realm of insentient things. If there were no Buddha-vehicle, there would be no Dharmakāya.
If one accepts that the essence is pervasive, one should not say that the body of the Buddha-dharma is identical to insentient things;

nor is it different from what is stated in the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, which says: "We now establish that the essence of the primary cause of sentient beings is pervasive," for the scriptural texts all employ space as a metaphor for it.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists everywhere, just like space."
Space is neither internal nor external; if it were both internal and external, how could it be called "all-pervading"? Since there are sentient beings everywhere, why does space not include them?
Thus, we know that the scriptural passage does not permit [space] to be exclusively internal or exclusively external.

Now, one may wonder: because the mind is all-pervasive, do insentient things such as grasses and trees attain Buddhahood? Should this be understood as the grasses and trees themselves attaining Buddhahood?

Because one cultivates the causes oneself, one attains Buddhahood; yet, if it is further claimed that plants and trees attain Buddhahood because the primary retribution (zhengbao) subsumes the secondary environment (yibao), how is this meaning to be understood?

If you say that plants and trees attain Buddhahood because the primary retribution subsumes the secondary environment, what difference is there between this and the School of Characteristics (xiangzong) which asserts that plants and trees attain Buddhahood by subsuming phenomena (xiang) into the nature (xing)? If you say that [the latter] does not speak of the external...

Regarding the statement that "form attains Buddhahood," if one speaks only of internal form attaining Buddhahood, this is identical to the Sanlun school’s claim that only those possessing a mind can attain Buddhahood, and not such things as walls or fences.

Furthermore, if it is said that because the Buddha-vehicle is established within insentient objects, grasses and trees naturally attain Buddhahood, then which specific grass or tree would personally cultivate the six perfections to achieve Buddhahood? How could this be explained?
"What is the principle of this analogy?
Tong said: "The myriad dharmas are mind-only; outside the mind there are no dharmas. The Dharma-realm, both the primary and secondary aspects, is fundamentally one body.
Therefore, apart from mind-only, there are no distinct characteristics of grasses or trees. It is only because of deluded thoughts and inverted views that one perceives what is not self or other."
Seeing self and other where there is neither "this" nor "that," one clings to the distinction between them; this clinging has become increasingly firm since beginningless time.

Consequently, regarding the non-dual essence, one stubbornly adheres to the difference between the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *āśrita*). Furthermore, when deluded about seeking the source, one fails to see that the three thousand realms of the environment and inhabitants are but the single mind.
Since the mind is without marks (*animitta*), all phenomena are likewise so. Where, then, do grasses, trees, and thickets arise? Vimalakīrti.
The *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "According as the mind is pure, so too is the Buddha-field pure. One who wishes to attain a pure land should purify their own mind.
If the mind and the land were different, then even if the mind were pure, the land would not be pure.
Because the mind and the land are non-dual, according as the mind is pure, so too is the Buddha-field pure. Truly knowing this, at the moment the Buddha-mind awakens, all phenomena are non-existent.

This is not the realization of the awakened ones. Now it is taught that the one mind is itself all dharmas, and all dharmas are themselves the one mind; therefore, based on this, both the environment and the mind are identical within the Single Buddha Vehicle.

This is why it differs from the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang*), which holds that the substance of mind and matter are distinct, and also differs from the Three Treatises school (*Sanlun*), which regards walls and other insentient things as non-sentient.
If deluded attachments are not eliminated, yet one seeks suffering [through asceticism] or attempts to personally cultivate the six perfections among grasses and trees, it is like using...

It is merely like those with diseased eyes seeking to see the fruit of empty flowers. Regarding the Dharma of the One Vehicle, in which the phenomenal world (*niṣyanda*) and the absolute reality (*dharmatā*) are non-dual:
those who awaken to it find the entire *dharmadhātu* transparently fused, while those who remain deluded find themselves separated from it at every turn.

Regarding the tenth point, the definitive meaning of the contemplation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) concerning whether the inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) of the Buddha-stage is severed or not, the *Yi-li* (Exemplary Meanings) states: "The Buddha fundamentally does not sever the dharma of inherent evil; therefore, if inherent evil were severed, from what would the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) arise?
The *Zhi-guan fu-xing-ji* (Sub-commentary on the Practice of Stopping and Contemplation) further explains: "The Tathāgata does not sever inherent evil. This clarifies [the point].

It is said that icchantikas do not sever innate goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*), and because they do not sever this innate goodness, it serves as the causal condition for their original existence. Furthermore, it is said:

"An icchantika severs cultivated goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*), yet innate goodness remains; likewise, a Tathāgata severs cultivated evil (*bhāvanā-akuśala*), yet innate evil remains. Now, a doubt arises:

at the ultimate stage of Buddhahood, when the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*) of the two obstacles have been permanently severed, how could there be any innate evil? If there were, [what would be its nature?]
If those whose nature is evil were to give rise to defiled practice, then the Buddha would fall into the evil realms.

If you say that the Tathāgata does not give rise to defiled practice nor fall into the evil realms because he has thoroughly realized the evil of his nature, is it that although the evil of nature exists, defiled practice does not arise because he has already fully realized this evil? Or is it that evil itself transforms into wisdom?

Therefore, cultivated evil does not arise. If it is argued that although the nature of evil exists, cultivated evil does not arise because one has already fully realized it as evil, then those who are bound by all fetters would also know this to be evil, and ordinary people (pṛthagjana) likewise should not give rise to evil.

If it is argued that cultivated evil does not arise because evil itself transforms into wisdom, then once the substance of evil has already become wisdom, [how could there be any further cultivation?]
Furthermore, what kind of nature of evil remains? If there were still evil, one could not say that the stage of Buddhahood is devoid of evil.
If there were still a nature of evil at the stage of Buddhahood, what would its mode of activity (*ākāra*) be like?
Is it like a staff or a mallet, which, despite their existence, never sprout branches and leaves; or is it like a single drop of ink on a white cloth? Regarding this meaning, it is as follows:

"What? [The questioner] asked. Tong replied: "The essential nature of good and evil is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. If one were to sever inherent evil (xing-è), one would be severing the three truths;

it would not be consistent to say that the Buddha severs inherent evil. If inherent evil were severed, the Tathāgata would lack the majestic deportment (wei-yi) of the Dharma-realm that manifests according to the various types of beings."
From where does manifestation arise? Furthermore, the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is itself bodhi;
this is clearly stated in the sutras. If one were to sever the nature of evil, one would sever bodhi. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not sever the nature of evil. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"The gates of both good and evil dharmas are all Buddha-dharma; it is by means of these dharmas that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas accomplish the work of Buddhahood. Thus, we truly know [this].
All evil deeds are the Buddha-dharma; within the dharma-realm there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma.
The Tathāgata’s clear illumination penetrates the dharma-realm of the three poisons, realizing that all evils are originally pure.

Having realized inconceivable liberation regarding evil, the Tathāgata does not sever his inherent nature of evil, yet he is not defiled by evil. Ordinary beings, however, know only that evil is unwholesome and do not...
To recognize all evils as empty, provisional, and middle, yet fail to perceive the principle of the Three Truths within evil, leads one to perpetually conceive of them as truly existent.
Consequently, one is constantly dragged about by various evils, unable to serve as an example for others and resulting in the formation of karmic bonds and difficulties.
One must know that all manifestations of the Imperial Net are precious jewels, and that the mutual fusion of the Dharma-realm is nothing other than the Three Truths. Thus it is understood.
The basis of the Uninterrupted [Hell] resides precisely within the Buddha’s own mind; it is not the body or land of the defiled and suffering *dharmakāya*.
This is because the minds of ordinary beings are eternally pure in every single thought-moment.

This is due to the fact that both good and evil take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their intrinsic nature, while the true mark, in turn, takes good and evil as its own phenomenal characteristics. Thus, both good and evil, at the stage of Buddhahood, are entirely the Buddha-realm.

The beauty and flaws of all images appear clearly and radiantly in a bright mirror. If one wishes to know the characteristics of the nature of evil within the Buddha-ground, it is like the characteristics of the Three Truths;
the nature of evil within the Buddha-realm is likewise characterized in this way.

This, indeed, cannot be proclaimed or measured by mind or speech, nor can it be illustrated by any worldly analogy. Yet, if one were to take a small portion and establish a forced analogy, it would be as follows:
It appears as the form of waves upon clear water, like the flavor of salt in water or the clarity of glue within colored lacquer.
This is an adornment of the Buddha-realm; though it may seem evil, it is always good, and thus cannot be called unwholesome.
